id_upper_fifth_canyon.blurb: A sport-leaning wall in the Q'emiln Park climbing zone beside Post Falls in North Idaho, set in a small canyon that you drop into from the park's main paths. Twenty routes, nearly all bolted, with a few trad and top-rope lines, mostly forty to sixty feet tall. Grades sit mainly in the 5.10s, with a good handful of 5.11s and only a few easier lines, so it suits climbers who are already comfortable on moderate to hard sport. The park's gneiss gives steep faces with positive holds. It sees fewer visitors than the park's closer walls, but the way down into the canyon is loose, so watch your footing, including while belaying.

id_pointless_crag.blurb: A compact cliff near Ririe in eastern Idaho, overlooking the Snake River's South Fork and reached along the river road east of Heise. Twenty climbs, nearly all sport, plus a single trad line and one top-rope. Grades start near 5.7, bunch up in the 5.10s and 5.11s, and finish with a few hard lines at the top end. Routes are short, and a stick-clip helps where the first bolt is high. The face looks southwest and the rock heats up in the sun, so cooler days suit it best. Some of the rock is loose, so wear a helmet and keep out of the fall zone. Rattlesnakes and ticks are around in warm months.

id_1_the_pit.blurb: A bolted wall on the rim of Teddy Bear Cove, near Massacre Rocks, with one of the quickest walks in from the car anywhere in the cove. All twenty routes are sport, from about 5.8 up to 5.13. The bulk are 5.11, with a solid group of 5.10s and a few 5.12s, which makes it a better stop for strong intermediates than for beginners. The lines are laid out along the cliff, and the first of them start almost at once past the gate. A helmet is a good idea, since loose rock between the lava flows is a known feature of the cove.

id_2_juniper_wall.blurb: A south-facing bolted wall at the top of Teddy Bear Cove, next to The Pit and close to Massacre Rocks. Twenty climbs: nineteen sport and one trad. The great majority fall in the 5.10s, with one easier route, a single 5.11, and a few 5.12s and a 5.13 at the top end. Juniper trees at the base shade a few lines and the belayers, but the wall is otherwise in the sun for most of the day, which makes this alcove a dependable winter pick. To get there, follow the base of the cliff along from The Pit until you reach a sandy bench where the routes begin.

id_hairpin_boulders.blurb: A small bouldering zone at Swan Falls on the Snake River, southwest of Boise, built around a lone egg-shaped basalt boulder at the bend in the road above the dam, with a few lower blocks nearby and a slab up the hill. Twenty problems run from very easy to a couple of hard V7 and V8 lines, though most are V0 to V3 with mostly flat landings. It is a short walk from a dirt pull-off. There is no tree shade, so spring, autumn and winter are the comfortable seasons, and crowds are rare.

il_henry_c_palmisano_nature_park.blurb: An urban bouldering stop inside a former limestone quarry park in the Bridgeport neighborhood of Chicago's Southwest Side. The climbing includes a purpose-built public boulder, a free place to try the sport without leaving the city, set among preserved quarry walls, a pond and walking paths. Most of the twenty-nine problems are V2 and V3, with a few easier ones and a handful up to about V5, so it works well for beginners, families and short sessions.

il_yosemite_slab.blurb: A cluster of sandstone boulders deep in the tight, forested canyon at Jackson Falls, in the Shawnee National Forest of southern Illinois. The walk in goes down the canyon, and downed trees can make it awkward. Twenty-nine problems span a wide range, from V0 up into the double digits, with the biggest group in the V5 to V7 range. The signature slab is about forty feet tall with few features and no protection, so a fall from high up is serious. The canyon holds plenty of shade, welcome in the hot, humid summers, and the fine-grained rock is strong.
